title: Interneurons Take the Long Way Round

scenes.tts: Most inhibitory neurons of the mouse cortex are not born in the cortex. The excitatory neurons are. They are made in the wall of the cortex, and climb straight out to their layers. So where do the inhibitory neurons come from?
scenes.visual: A cortical wall; orange inhibitory cells sit in it, blue excitatory cells are born at the bottom and climb up; a question mark with dashed arrow stands outside the wall.
scenes.narration: Most inhibitory neurons of the mouse cortex are not born in the cortex. The excitatory neurons are. They are made in the wall of the cortex, and climb straight out to their layers. So where do the inhibitory neurons come from?

scenes.tts: They start lower, in the ventral forebrain, in swellings called the ganglionic eminences. These are temporary zones packed with dividing progenitors. In cultured rat embryos, dye placed there labels some cells that run sideways into the cortex. In mouse embryos lacking both D L X one and D L X two, the cells make no such trip. The cortex ends up with few inhibitory neurons.
scenes.caption: They start lower, in the ventral forebrain, in swellings called the ganglionic eminences. These are temporary zones packed with dividing progenitors. In cultured rat embryos, dye placed there labels some cells that run sideways into the cortex. In mouse embryos lacking both Dlx1 and Dlx2, the cells make no such trip. scenes.visual: The question mark becomes the eminence; dye patch, labelled cells run sideways into the wall; then a Dlx1/Dlx2 mutant: cells stay put, cortex nearly empty.
scenes.narration: They start lower, in the ventral forebrain, in swellings called the ganglionic eminences. These are temporary zones packed with dividing progenitors. In cultured rat embryos, dye placed there labels some cells that run sideways into the cortex. In mouse embryos lacking both Dlx1 and Dlx2, the cells make no such trip. The cortex ends up with few inhibitory neurons.

scenes.tts: A pyramidal neuron moves at right angles to the surface, mostly by gripping a radial glial fibre. An interneuron moves parallel to the surface, with no glial fibre to follow. Early on, in the cortex, interneurons travel in two streams. One runs just beneath the meninges. The other runs deep in the wall. Between them, the young cortical plate holds few interneurons early on.
scenes.visual: A blue cell climbs a fibre; an orange cell crosses sideways with no fibre; then two orange streams fill the superficial and deep lanes, the plate between them nearly empty.
scenes.narration: A pyramidal neuron moves at right angles to the surface, mostly by gripping a radial glial fibre. An interneuron moves parallel to the surface, with no glial fibre to follow. Early on, in the cortex, interneurons travel in two streams. One runs just beneath the meninges. The other runs deep in the wall. Between them, the young cortical plate holds few interneurons early on.

scenes.tts: Why do cells stay in the streams, instead of diving into the plate at once? Chemokines are small secreted proteins, first known for steering immune cells. One chemokine, called C X C L 12, lines both streams. The meninges make it, and so do dividing precursors in the deep wall. The interneurons carry its receptor, C X C R 4. In a chamber assay, striatal precursor cells moved toward it, but not when it was added equally on both sides.
scenes.caption: Why do cells stay in the streams, instead of diving into the plate at once? Chemokines are small secreted proteins, first known for steering immune cells. One chemokine, called CXCL12, lines both streams. The meninges make it, and so do dividing precursors in the deep wall. The interneurons carry its receptor, CXCR4. In a chamber assay, striatal precursor cells moved toward it, but not when it was added equally on both sides.
scenes.visual: Teal dots appear along both lanes (meninges, deep precursors); cells gain a receptor tab; then two chambers: cells cross toward chemokine below, stay put when it is on both sides.
scenes.narration: Why do cells stay in the streams, instead of diving into the plate at once? Chemokines are small secreted proteins, first known for steering immune cells. One chemokine, called CXCL12, lines both streams. The meninges make it, and so do dividing precursors in the deep wall. The interneurons carry its receptor, CXCR4. In a chamber assay, striatal precursor cells moved toward it, but not when it was added equally on both sides.

scenes.tts: Take away the receptor, and the cells leave their streams. They enter the cortical plate early, and they spread less widely across the cortex. The chemokine controls retention, timing and spread. Normally, a cell seems to stop answering C X C L 12 to leave a stream. Then it turns into the plate, toward its layer.

The chemokine controls retention, timing and spread. Normally, a cell seems to stop answering CXCL12 to leave a stream. Then it turns into the plate, toward its layer.
scenes.visual: No-receptor case: cells drop from the lanes early near the entrance. Reset to normal; one cell's receptor tab fades, and only then does it turn into the plate.
scenes.narration: Take away the receptor, and the cells leave their streams. They enter the cortical plate early, and they spread less widely across the cortex. The chemokine controls retention, timing and spread. Normally, a cell seems to stop answering CXCL12 to leave a stream. Then it turns into the plate, toward its layer.

scenes.tts: So the long way round is a series of decisions. In mice, most interneurons are born outside the cortex, and travel sideways. A chemokine keeps them in their lanes. Keep this rule. Cells seem to stay on the route until they stop answering the signal.
scenes.visual: One cell travels eminence, lane, then into the plate; three chips mark the steps.
